paper_title: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone's pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to-fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this with length-aware global batching and cross-GPU load balancing, raising training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. Built on Qwen3.5-4B and trained on 12.3M question-answer pairs converted from existing spatial datasets, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score (65.64%) among eight tested models, ranks first on seven of twelve benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve, while running 2.5 times faster than the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 times faster than the base model.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Spatial intelligence involves perceiving and reasoning about the geometry and spatial relationships of objects,
which enables agents to navigate their surroundings and interact with the physical world (Chen et al., 2024;
Cheng et al., 2024). Many of these interactions require timely spatial judgments. Vision-language models
(VLMs) support these capabilities by answering spatial questions grounded in visual observations. Such
questions may require selecting an option that describes a spatial relation (Ray et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2024;
Fu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026), estimating a numerical quantity such as distance (Cai et al., 2026; Yang
et al., 2025a,b), or identifying a point for object placement (Zhou et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2024; Song et al.,
2025; Cheng et al., 2025).
sections.content: To produce these spatial predictions, many existing VLMs retain their pretrained autoregressive textgeneration capabilities (Chen et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024; Deitke et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a). Each option, numerical value, or image location is therefore represented as token sequence that the model is trained to reproduce. This couples learning the spatial answer with learning its textual form, including formatting and boilerplate when present, introducing supervision beyond the task-relevant prediction itself. At inference, the model must generate the answer tokens sequentially, after which the resulting text must be parsed to recover the spatial prediction, adding decoding and parsing overhead. This motivates System 1 approach to spatial understanding: using pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to make spatial judgments directly. Jev provides precedent for this approach by returning probabilities over specified candidates without generating answer text (TypeSafe AI, 2026). At the same time, we observe that all three common spatial output types can be represented as finite candidate sets: answer options are already finite, while numerical values and image locations can be discretized within specified range and resolution. Building on these insights, we introduce MJev-Spatial, multimodal decision model specifically tailored to spatial understanding. MJev-Spatial unifies the three output types by casting prediction as classification over finite candidate sets. Each class represents supplied answer option, numerical bin, or an image region, depending on the task. Selecting class gives the chosen option, predicts which bin contains the target value, or predicts which region contains the target point. To choose among these classes, MJev-Spatial encodes their descriptions together with the observation and question, then reuses the final attention layers pretrained query and key projections to compute class scores. softmax over these scores gives the class probabilities, without additional prediction heads or trainable parameters. At inference, each classification decision scores all its candidates in one forward pass. Furthermore, to obtain fine-grained values and coordinates without evaluating large number of classes at once, we subdivide the selected numerical bin or image region and classify again. Numerical prediction uses up to two stages; single-point prediction uses three stages, re-encoding the selected image crop before each later decision to recover local visual detail. The final selection is decoded to numerical value or image coordinates. Conditional tree expansion evaluates multiple region paths to extend the same trained point predictor to multiple points without additional training. Numerical and point prediction can require multiple supervised stages, with new image crops introduced between point decisions. Ground-truth answers determine the target classes and crops, allowing all stages to be jointly supervised in one teacher-forced causal forward pass. We average the stage cross-entropy losses per question so that multi-stage example does not receive greater weight than one-stage choice. Global length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing address the padding and workload imbalance caused by different sequence lengths and crop counts while preserving optimizer-batch membership. An audited conversion pipeline supplies 12.3M QA from existing spatial annotations for full-parameter training of the retained language backbone. Built on Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score among eight evaluated models, leads on seven benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve. Across all twelve benchmarks, it achieves 2.5 and 5.6 speedups over the fastest autoregressive baseline and the base model, respectively. Separate studies examine candidate scoring, visual refinement, numerical discretization, and training execution. The readout and refinement studies assess how candidate scoring with pretrained projections and crop re-encoding contribute to prediction quality and computational cost; the numerical study shows that coarser length discretization can reduce prediction error despite its lower resolution. Global length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing further improve training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. 2 Our contributions are as follows: (1) We propose novel System 1 paradigm for spatial intelligence, unifying option selection, numerical estimation, and image pointing through direct classification over finite candidate sets. (2) Building on this paradigm, we develop MJev-Spatial and unified training recipe, using pretrained attention projections for candidate scoring and joint supervision across spatial tasks and refinement stages. (3) Across twelve spatial benchmarks, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest mean score among eight evaluated models and 5.6 speedup over its autoregressive base model, Qwen3.5-4B.

2 Related Work
System 1 decision model. Jev motivates predicting over declared answer spaces instead of generating
unrestricted answer text (TypeSafe AI, 2026). Jev-Omni extends this interface to multimodal inputs (akhi-
laaa3, 2026), while KEV implements candidate scoring with learned query and key projections (Palmer,
2026). Yu and Yao (2026) and hr98w (2026) study direct decisions and shared-context execution; FBddcz
and EmbodiedJev contributors (2026) applies decision interfaces to skill and action selection. Concurrent
work, VideoJev, uses a shared candidate scorer for temporal grounding and video question answering, with
cached and joint inference for queries about the same video (Zhu et al., 2026a). Visual Jev reads candidate-
token probabilities from the existing language-model head and finds no consistent accuracy advantage from
an added typed head in its matched control. MJev-Spatial instead scores contextual candidate content with
the backbone’s final-layer query and key projections and trains all output types with the same candidate-
classification objective. Our matched readout experiments show competitive quality and lower training cost
for this design, with task-dependent tradeoffs (Section 4.3). The earlier Molmo2-ER-based MJev-Spatial
prototype used LoRA and an added decision head (Fang et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2022). The present model
uses Qwen3.5-4B and trains all retained language parameters. Backbone efficiency is also studied through
pruning and quantization, joint low-rank and sparsity optimization, and adaptive execution (Zhou et al.,
2026a,b, 2025b,c).
sections.content: Class-aware adaptation provides complementary route to efficient vision-language classification. AWT enriches class descriptions and combines augmented views through entropy-based weighting and optimal transport (Zhu et al., 2024a). Self-TPT uses self-supervised prompt adaptation for new classes to avoid costly per-image optimization at inference (Zhu et al., 2026b). Spatial understanding with VLMs. Broader multimodal research covers visual reasoning (Qin et al., 2025), retrieval (Qin et al., 2024), and multimodal generation (Zhang et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2026; Zhong et al., 2025). Video understanding further requires temporal localization (Zhu et al., 2024b, 2026c) and efficient processing of long or streaming observations (Li et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026a). SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT learn spatial relations and numerical answers from spatial supervision (Chen et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024), while Molmo, RoboPoint, and RoboRefer support pointing through coordinate text (Deitke et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a). Alternative interfaces can ground predictions more directly. MolmoPoint selects visual patches and refines locations through sequence of specialized grounding tokens (Clark et al., 2026). MJev-Spatial uses one candidate-classification mechanism for options, numerical values, and points, with task-specific candidates supplying the output structure. Its multi-point extension expands conditional classification paths rather than generating variable-length coordinate string. Representing continuous predictions with discrete classes is established in computer vision. DORN formulates monocular depth estimation as ordinal regression over logarithmically spaced depth intervals (Fu et al., 2018). Our length representation also uses logarithmically spaced coarse intervals, followed by linear refinement, but its intervals are candidate descriptions scored by shared language backbone. Counts and angles retain their own ranges and discretization schemes. Visual search methods such as refine image regions to recover details needed for answering (Wu and Xie, 2024). Video-o3 similarly acquires evidence iteratively in long videos, interleaving clue seeking with inspection of relevant segments (Zeng et al., 2026b). In MJev-Spatial, region selection itself is supervised as classification, and re-encoded crops provide the evidence for subsequent decisions. 3 Figure 2. Task formulation and coarse-to-fine inference. Every stage uses shared candidate scorer. Choice tasks select supplied option. Numerical estimation selects coarse interval and then fine interval, returning its midpoint. Point prediction uses three 3 3 region selections, re-encoding crops between stages and returning the final cell center.

Given ordered images I = (I1, . . . , Im) and a spatial question q, the model predicts an option, a number with
a declared unit, or a point in normalized image coordinates. Each candidate is a possible answer for the
current decision. For a choice question, it is one of the supplied options; for a numerical or point question, it
identifies an interval or region in which the target is predicted to lie. This lets all three output types use the
same candidate-classification rule.

3.2 Model Architecture
The framework in Section 3.1 defines the candidate classes and refinement rules; a model must still deter-
mine which class is supported by the visual observation and question. Following Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026), we
adapt a pretrained VLM to make these decisions. Its contextual representations draw on visual and linguistic
knowledge acquired during large-scale pretraining, providing a basis for interpreting the scene and evaluating
possible answers. We build on this capacity by formulating classification as matching a decision representa-
tion with candidate representations. Our design reuses both pretrained features and matching projections,

Each candidate is expressed as text: choice tasks retain the supplied option content, numerical tasks specify values or intervals with their units, and pointing tasks name cells relative to the current image region, such as top-left or center. These descriptions provide the candidate content that the VLM contextualizes with the observation and question. We instantiate MJev-Spatial with Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026). Its vision encoder and merger convert the images into visual tokens, which are encoded together with the question, preceding refinement history, and current candidate descriptions in causal sequence. Each candidate description ends with an option-end marker, and the complete candidate list ends with decision marker. After the first 31 language layers, the hidden state at each option-end marker represents that candidate in the context of the observation, question, and preceding candidates. The hidden state at the decision marker incorporates the full candidate set and serves as the decision representation. The markers reuse existing vocabulary entries, so no new embeddings are introduced. Section A.2 gives the exact sequence layout. 3.3 Training Recipe
We convert existing spatial annotations into 12.3M training QA and supervise all refinement stages of each
question in one language-backbone forward pass. Length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing reduce
padding and workload imbalance.
sections.content: Training data. Our training corpus contains 12.3M questionanswer pairs converted from RefSpatial (Zhou et al., 2025a), SAT (Ray et al., 2025), SenseNova-SI (Cai et al., 2026), VSI-590K-image (Yang et al., 2025a), and VST-P (Yang et al., 2025b). The training data cover multiple-choice spatial question answering (7.1M QA), point localization (3.5M QA), length estimation (1.6M QA), angle estimation (120K QA), and counting (38K QA). These totals count original QA before expansion into decision stages. See Table 7 in Appendix for the source-by-task breakdown, with conversion and validation details provided in the same appendix. Joint stage supervision. Every supervised decision uses categorical cross-entropy over its current candidate set. choice question has one target class, whereas numerical and point questions can contain sequence of target classes; point refinement also introduces image crops between stages. The annotated answer determines the complete target path and any corresponding crops before training. We serialize the stages in causal order, with each target choice and any subsequent crop placed after the corresponding decision position. Earlier decisions therefore cannot attend to later choices or crops, while teacher forcing allows all stage losses to be evaluated in single language-backbone forward pass. Joint supervision removes the need for separate language-backbone training pass at each refinement stage, but questions still require different amounts of computation. In particular, point examples add two image crops, while choice and numerical examples have different candidate lengths and stage counts. Padding dissimilar sequences wastes work, and assigning unequal work to GPUs delays synchronization. We sort the expanded sequences within each global optimizer batch by length to form similar-length microbatches. longest-work-first assignment (Graham, 1969) then distributes the microbatches across GPUs, using cost that accounts for padded sequence length and visual-token work. This combines length grouping with cross-GPU load balancing while preserving the questions in each optimizer batch and their weights in Equation (7). The assignment rule and distributed normalization are specified in Section C.3. Given the scale of our expanded training corpus, we adopt full-parameter fine-tuning of the language backbone, although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is also applicable (Zhou et al., 2025d, 2026c, 2025e,f, 2026d). The final configuration uses eight GPUs, per-device microbatch size of eight, and eight gradient accumulation steps, yielding global batch size of 512. We use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rates of 5 106 for the backbone and 2 104 for the readout. Language computation uses BF16, while trainable weights, gradients, optimizer states, and candidate scoring remain in FP32. The vision encoder and merger are frozen. MJev-Spatial is compared with seven generative baselines: Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), Qwen3-VL-8B-
Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025), InternVL3.5-8B (Wang et al., 2025), Molmo2-ER (Fang et al., 2026), Spatial-
sections.content: 8 SSRL (Liu et al., 2025), SenseNova-SI (Cai et al., 2026), and SpatialThinker (Batra et al., 2025). Our evaluation covers the popular SAT (Ray et al., 2025), CV-Bench (Tong et al., 2024), BLINK (Fu et al., 2024), MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2026), RefSpatial-Bench (Zhou et al., 2025a), Where2Place (Yuan et al., 2024), Point-Bench (Cheng et al., 2025), RoboSpatial VQA and pointing (Song et al., 2025), ERQA (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025), EmbSpatial (Du et al., 2024), and VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025d). For model-design ablations, we use fixed 72K-QA mixture of 25K SAT choice questions, 22K VST-P length questions, and 25K RefSpatial point questions to reduce training cost while providing sufficient supervision for meaningful comparisons. Each model is trained for 2.2K updates using the same optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and image-token budgets. VST-300 serves as the development set for length estimation.

sections.title:
4.2 Main Result
Our main evaluation tests the central premise of MJev-Spatial: a System 1 decision model can make accurate
spatial judgments with low inference latency. We therefore assess prediction quality and latency jointly,
comparing MJev-Spatial with seven autoregressive VLMs.
sections.content: MJev-Spatial achieves the highest average score of 65.64%, ahead of 62.79% for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and ranks first on seven of the twelve benchmarks  (Table 2)  . It also outperforms its autoregressive base model on all twelve benchmarks, including gains of 22.89 percentage points on RoboSpatial VQA and 12.50 points on RefSpatial-Bench. These improvements span both spatial question answering and point localization. For length estimation, the final model reaches an MAE of 0.103 on the VST-300 development set. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, MJev-Spatial also achieves the lowest mean query latency, 160.6 ms, yielding 2.5 speedup over the fastest autoregressive baseline and 5.6 speedup over its base model  (Table 11)  . The combination of the highest average score and lowest mean latency gives MJev-Spatial the strongest performance latency trade-off among the compared models (Figure 1). These results support our System 1 approach to spatial understanding: adapting pretrained multimodal knowledge into direct classification decisions that deliver both strong prediction quality and fast responses.

sections.title:
4.3 Ablation Studies
We next examine the design choices that make direct classification effective across spatial tasks. The studies
follow the prediction process: we first assess the shared candidate-scoring mechanism, then examine how
numerical discretization and visual refinement provide the precision needed for value and point prediction.
We further study how decoding adapts these predictions to different output requirements, including multiple
points. This progression connects the common classifier to the task-specific decisions behind the final model.

We compare native Q/K scoring with typical linear classifier and KEV (Palmer, 2026) pointer using newly initialized projections to assess whether adding prediction head improves over reusing the pretrained projections  (Table 3)  . Multi-point prediction. Finally, we test whether the same point-classification hierarchy can recover multiple targets without additional training. Replacing repeated continue/stop decisions with spatial probability tree raises Point-Bench counting success from 19.39% to 38.78%  (Table 21)  . sections.title:
4.4 Training Speed
The scheduling study tests whether similar-length microbatches and cross-GPU workload balancing reduce
the cost of training heterogeneous spatial questions. Four fresh runs use the same historical 72K corpus,
global batch 256, microbatch eight, four accumulation steps, and eight L20D GPUs. Each runs 100 updates;
after eight warmup updates, the measurement window contains the same 23,552 QA. The comparison holds
the model and training computation fixed apart from scheduling.
sections.content: Local length grouping raises throughput from 99.06 to 116.91 QA/s and reduces padding from 35.17% to 12.36%, but increases mean gradient-ready spread from 115.0 to 306.6 ms  (Table 6)  . Global grouping with cross-GPU balancing reduces padding to 1.77% and ready-time spread to 145.7 ms, reaching 129.54 QA/s: 30.78% higher throughput, or 23.53% less measured time for the same QA volume, than the original strategy. Since ready-time spread remains above the original value, the gain reflects the combined scheduling change. 128-QA cross-update buffer lowers padding to 1.03% but does not improve throughput and increases steptime variability. We retain the unbuffered layout to preserve optimizer-batch membership. Distributed checks verify per-question loss normalization with unequal workloads and incomplete tails, without implying bitwise equivalence across BF16 batch shapes. These short runs measure throughput, not convergence or full-run duration; they include no downstream quality evaluation. Full timing and batch-size feasibility profiles appear in Section H.

sections.title:
5 Conclusion
MJev-Spatial investigates a System One approach to spatial understanding: using pretrained multimodal
knowledge to make direct spatial decisions without generating answer text. Options, numerical values, and
image locations share a candidate-classification mechanism, with hierarchical refinement providing numerical
and spatial precision and tree expansion extending point prediction without further training. An audited
12.3M-QA corpus and joint stage supervision support training across these tasks; length grouping and cross-
GPU balancing improve throughput by 30.8% in a controlled eight-GPU study. The final Qwen3.5-4B-based
model achieves the highest overall score, leads seven of twelve reported metrics among eight evaluated models,
and exceeds its local autoregressive base model on all twelve. Its mean batch-one query latency is 160.6 ms
across the twelve benchmarks, giving 2.5× and 5.6× speedups over the fastest autoregressive baseline and
the base model under the reported timing protocol. Together with the controlled design studies, these results
support direct candidate decisions as a viable approach to the spatial tasks studied here.

sections.content: A.1 Autoregressive Reference and Decision Paths Problem setup. Given ordered images = (I1, . . . , Im) and spatial question q, the goal is to predict typed answer Yq: one of the supplied options, number with declared unit, or location in normalized image coordinates. In an autoregressive formulation, vision-language model πθ generates an answer string = (w1, . . . , wL) autoregressively, πθ(w I, q) = (cid:89) l=1 πθ(wl I, q, w<l), (8) and task-specific parser then maps to y. Answer generation therefore adds sequential decoding steps whose number depends on the output length L. In the classification formulation, the state at stage is st = (I, q, h<t), where h<t contains the preceding selections and visual refinements. deterministic controller constructs Ct, advances the state after selection, and decodes the terminal path to the required answer. For fixed observation and question, reachable states form finite tree of depth at most three, with path probability (a1:S I, q) = (cid:89) t=1 pθ(at I, q, h<t, Ct). (9) Ordinary decoding follows the greedy path in Equation (1); multi-point decoding expands several spatial paths. Training supervises all annotated transitions using Equation (7). Each textual decision supports up to 32 candidates, with padded slots masked before normalization. A.2 Input Sequence and Candidate Representations Sequence layout. Each questionanswer example (QA) is represented by an image prefix followed by the question, candidate descriptions, and decision marker: [state, I1, . . . , Im, question, q, opt, c1, end, . . . , opt, cK, end, decide]. (10) The sequence markers reuse existing vocabulary entries, leaving the vocabulary and embedding matrix unchanged. Candidate representations. The frozen vision encoder (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) and merger embed each image into the language sequence, and the first 31 language layers contextualize the whole causal row. The state at an option-end marker then summarizes that option in the context of the image, the question, and the preceding options, while the state at the decision marker sees all current candidates. Changing an option therefore changes its representation rather than the interpretation of fixed classifier slot, which lets the candidate set vary freely across questions. Training shuffles candidate order, while evaluation follows each benchmarks ordering protocol. Multi-stage rows. Each QA occupies its own causal row. later stage appends the selected option, an optional new image crop, and new question and candidate block. During training, all supervised stages fit in one teacher-forced (Williams and Zipser, 1989) causal sequence. Each decision marker precedes the later choices and crops, so one forward pass supervises every stage without showing future crop to an earlier decision. At inference, the next stage is constructed only after the current prediction. A.3 Candidate Scoring with Pretrained Query and Key Projections The shared scorer produces one class logit for each current candidate. The final full-attention layers pretrained query projection acts on the decision state, and its key projection acts on each candidate state; comparing the resulting vectors gives the logits used in Equation (1). This reuses existing parameters to compute classification scores without an additional prediction head. 17 Backbone boundary. Qwen3.5-4B has 32 language layers with hidden width = 2560. Full attention occurs at L4, L8, . . . , L32, and the other 24 layers are Gated DeltaNet. We run L1L31, including their residual and feed-forward paths, and read representations at the input to L32. full-attention layer has = 16 query heads, = 4 key/value heads, and head width = 256. Querykey scoring. Let ut R2560 be the L32 input state at the decision marker of stage t, and vt,i R2560 the state at the option-end marker of candidate i. With the native input RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019) Nin, the headwise RMSNorms NQ, NK, and the partial rotary operator (Su et al., 2024) Rp, the logits are Qt,h = Rpt (cid:104) Kt,i,g = Rpt,i (cid:16) NQ (cid:104) NK (h) (cid:16) Nin(ut) (g) Nin(vt,i) (cid:17)(cid:105) , (cid:17)(cid:105) st,h,i = t,hKt,i,g(h) 256 , zt,i = 1 16 15 (cid:88) h=0 st,h,i. , = 0, . . . , 15, = 0, . . . , 3, g(h) = h/4, (11) (12) (13) (14) The rotary positions are the original token positions of the gathered states. Qwens multimodal rotary embedding (Wang et al., 2024) rotates the first 64 coordinates of each head and leaves the other 192 unchanged. Each group of four query heads shares one key head, as in grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023). The score is learned, position-aware scaled inner product. We average the head logits and apply single softmax over the legal candidates. The candidate probability is Equation (1), with only the current alternatives in the denominator. Each logit thus decomposes into 16 head contributions, which the intervention analysis in Section E.4 exploits. Reusing the pretrained projections. Qwens projection is bias-free 2560 8192 matrix whose 512 output rows per head hold 256-dimensional query followed by 256-dimensional output gate. The readout uses the 256 query dimensions of each head, giving WQ R40962560. The key projection WK R10242560 and both head norms are kept as they are. All of these parameters start from the official pretrained checkpoint. Removing unused computation. Since the readout sits before the value aggregation and residual update of L32, the projection, output-gate rows, output projection, post-attention norm, and SwiGLU FFN (Shazeer, 2020) of L32, together with the final language-model norm, have no path to the loss and are removed. Earlier layers stay intact. The readout gathers the decision states and (cid:80) Kt option-end states before projecting them, so it forms neither full-sequence Q/K projection nor an attention matrix. Its candidate-comparison work is O((cid:80) KtHd), while image encoding and the L1L31 prefill still scale with the full input length. The retained language model has 4,111,374,336 trainable parameters, 95,688,192 fewer than the completelanguage KEV model; the removed FFN alone accounts for 70,778,880. The Q/K projections and their head norms, 13,107,712 parameters, form the readout optimizer group, and the input norm stays in the backbone group. Trainable weights, gradients, Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) states, and all readout operations use FP32, while the retained language layers compute in BF16, following standard mixed-precision training (Micikevicius et al., 2018; Kalamkar et al., 2019). The vision encoder and merger stay frozen in BF16. This keeps the small candidate comparison numerically stable while the backbone computation, which dominates the cost, runs in mixed precision. A.4 Multi-Point Decoding Rules For Point-Bench counting, the same trained model supplies three-level conditional probability tree, pθ(at I, q, a<t), (15) (a1:3 I, q) = 3 (cid:89) t=1 whose complete expansion visits 1 + 9 + 81 = 91 decision nodes and produces 729 cells. For evaluation, we drop first-level branch only when p(a1) < 0.01 maxj p(j), so each retained root adds ten decision nodes and 81 leaf cells, and deeper levels are fully expanded. Unvisited cells remain unknown, and the omitted mass is recorded without renormalizing the retained probabilities. On the resulting map, cells above 10% of the retained global peak form an eight-connected superlevel set, and each connected component outputs the center of its peak cell. The threshold, connectivity, and root cutoff are fixed without test labels; target masks and true point counts are used only by the scorer. This turns distributed spatial mass into variable number of points without learned stop decision or ground-truth top-k. The tree costs more than the three-node pointing path, and its pruning and decoder sensitivities are measured in Section F.2.

sections.title: B Data Conversion and Validation
sections.content: B.1 From Spatial Annotations to Classification Supervision We convert spatial annotations from the training collection curated for Molmo2-ER (Fang et al., 2026), which contains 5M source records and 21.1M QA. The annotations originate from RefSpatial (Zhou et al., 2025a), SAT (Ray et al., 2025), SenseNova-SI (Cai et al., 2026), VSI-590K (Yang et al., 2025a), VST-P (Yang et al., 2025b), and RoboPoint (Yuan et al., 2024); Table 7 reports their contributions to the final corpus. Each accepted QA contains the ordered images, question, answer type, candidates, and target. Supplied options retain their semantic content, numerical labels determine the target intervals, and point coordinates determine the target regions and training crops. Source answers and rationales are excluded from model inputs. Answer options. Supplied text and image options are retained when exactly one candidate matches the source answer. Questions with ambiguous matches or unresolved image bindings are excluded. Question text, including comparison clauses, is preserved separately from the candidate descriptions. Numerical supervision. When no explicit answer menu applies, the requested quantity determines the task and units. Length targets are converted to meters, counts are exact integers in 01023, and angle direction follows the question. We accept scalar target only when its value and unit are unambiguous. Ranges, inequalities, conflicting quantities, and unsupported area or volume answers are excluded. Point and relation supervision. Single-point labels with verified coordinate convention are normalized to the original image. Multiple-point lists, region-only annotations, unresolved image bindings, and examples with more than five source images are excluded. Boolean and relation labels use fixed candidate vocabularies when no supplied answer menu applies. RoboPoint-spatial (Yuan et al., 2024) contributes no final QA because its available multi-point or region supervision is outside this adaptation. B.2 Data Quality Checks We compare 245 converted numerical QA with their source annotations and semantically review 75 cases. targeted review of 66,574 QA with known option-conversion issues recovers 65,902 QA and excludes 672 ambiguous cases. We remove adapter-added option labels and answer-format instructions while preserving the meaning of candidate text. This cleanup affects 15.2M candidate texts across 6.5M QA; the final corpus contains 12,304,058 QA. We check 3,422 nontrivial cleanup cases against their source annotations and validate 3,427 rendered training examples across five sources and 200 display categories, including teacher-forced crops. focused content review examines 393 cases. Another 256 pointing questions are flagged for coordinate-wording review. B.3 Duplicate Filtering and Evaluation Separation We exclude invalid images and training examples whose images exactly match public evaluation images or satisfy conservative near-duplicate criterion. Near-duplicates require 64-bit difference-hash (Krawetz, 2013) Hamming distance at most 2, aspect ratios within 1%, and mean absolute RGB difference at most 6 on 8 8 thumbnails. These checks target nearly identical images; they do not establish physical-scene or video-neighbor independence. 19 Image validation covers 2.1M image identities and excludes 85 images. Conflicting targets for the same input cause all members of that group to be excluded, while identical duplicate examples are reduced to one. The filtering stages exclude 45,820 duplicate-input QA, 3,430 QA with conflicting targets, and 201 near-duplicate QA under the public-test policy. Examples whose estimated training sequences exceed 4,096 tokens, including refinement crops, are excluded. sections.content: C.1 Matched 72K Training Recipe The controlled studies use 72K QA: 25K choice questions from SAT (Ray et al., 2025), 22K length-estimation questions from VST-P (Yang et al., 2025b), and 25K pointing questions from RefSpatial (Zhou et al., 2025a). The length subset contains 11K height and 11K longest-dimension labels, ranging from 0 to 167.82 m. Examples, order, and one-pass exposure budget are fixed for the matched comparisons. The aligned experiments use eight NVIDIA L20D GPUs, four QA per GPU, global batch 32, no gradient accumulation, and 2,252 optimizer updates for one pass. For the selected native model, this pass takes 1,413 of training time (3.14 GPU-hours). All three primary readout models share seed 3407, the canonical QA permutation, image budgets, stage-normalized loss, and optimizer settings. Vision and merger parameters are frozen; retained language parameters are fully trainable. Training allows 64512 visual tokens per image and at most 4,096 to20 tal tokens per QA sequence. Shared language prefixes and visual deduplication are disabled for this controlled comparison. Fused AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) uses β = (0.9, 0.95), ϵ = 108, global gradient-norm clipping (Pascanu et al., 2013) at 1, and weight decay 0.01 on the backbone and 0 on the readout. sections.title: E Extended Readout Studies
sections.content: E.1 Readout Controls and Optimization Alignment We test whether pretrained candidate scorer can replace an added classification head while retaining competitive spatial performance. The controlled comparison evaluates three ways to convert contextual representations into candidate scores. position classifier applies LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016) and 32output linear layer to the decision state; its outputs refer to candidate slots. KEV pointer completes the language backbone and projects the decision and option-end states with two newly initialized affine 2560 256 maps, scoring their dot product divided by 256. It adds 1,311,232 parameters and explicitly represents candidate content. The native mean model instead reuses the final attention projections at the earlier boundary in Section 3.2. The comparison therefore tests both representation source and the amount of downstream computation retained. Table 3 is the primary matched readout comparison. Native mean improves over the linear classifier by 1.58 points on CV-Bench, 7.72 on RoboSpatial VQA, and 2.00 on RefSpatial; MAE falls by 8.93%. The gains come with losses of 8.01 points on Where2Place and 3.28 on RoboSpatial pointing. Relative to KEV, native mean improves RefSpatial and length error but is not uniformly better on choice tasks. Its retained parameter count and measured training cost are lower. These results support pretrained candidate scoring as compact shared design; they do not establish that its scoring formula alone causes every gain, since templates and initialization source remain architecture-dependent. 23 Table 12. Hierarchical point classification must preserve enough visual detail to distinguish increasingly small regions. We therefore separate three questions: whether crop-trained weights can operate without crops, whether matching training to cheaper visual input recovers quality, and whether spatial candidates should be text regions or visual tokens. sections.content: G.1 Numerical Design: Coverage, Granularity, and Decoding Numerical discretization has two sources of error: representing true value with finite cell center, and predicting the correct cell from the image. The following experiments measure these separately. Codebook candidates are designed from training labels, and the 4/8 codebook below is used for the final model. All learned comparisons, however, retain the old 72K-QA gradient-training budget, including only 22K length examples. Coverage comes before precision. The historical codebook has 12 positive intervals ending at 200 m, two special roots, and 32 fine cells per positive interval. It covers all old 72K length labels but overflows on 12K expanded-corpus labels. The scale audit compares uniform, log, quantile, task-specific, and hierarchical allocations on all 1.6M accepted lengths  (Table 25)  . These are label encode/decode oracles, assuming every classification decision is correct. Uniform 960-cell spacing up to 16,384 gives MAE 6.4545 because most labels are short. Quantile spacing improves the proportion within 1 cm to 80.78%, yet produces MAE 4.2371 and maximum error 3935.55 m: dense central distribution leaves the sparse tail poorly represented. Shared log allocations balance these scales more effectively. The 30-by-32 two-stage log1p proposal reaches 0.0391 oracle MAE and 21.39 maximum error, compared with 1.6548 and 8320.10 for the historical codebook. Task-specific log allocation offers 33 small average improvement but introduces question-type routing and poorly supported rare categories (e.g., only five diameter and four thickness labels). We therefore keep shared length codebook and the existing linear within-interval decoder. Testing the 30-by-32 proposal as model. new L32 mean model uses 30 positive log1p intervals and 32 fine cells per interval (960 leaves), preserving all other 72K settings and the exact non-numerical stage texts and mappings. On those training labels, oracle MAE falls from 0.006591 to 0.003891 and P99 error from 0.045625 to 0.023542 m, but worst-case error rises from 0.7475 to 0.9800 m. The new numerical candidate text adds 527.43 tokens on average; the longest checked scalar sequence is 2,068 tokens, within the 4,096-token budget. Coverage and average quantization improve at real input-cost increase. The learned model reduces VST-300 MAE from 0.335420 to 0.327732 m, only 2.29%, and lowers all five classification benchmark scores. The much larger oracle gain does not translate directly into prediction accuracy. This motivates reducing fine-stage difficulty rather than adding still more representational resolution. Reducing the fine-stage candidate count. The 4/8 design in Equation (3) keeps the same coarse intervals and range but reduces positive leaves from 960 to 216. In the full length census, 108K positive labels use four fine candidates, 1.5M use eight, and 382 terminate at zero. Both the 32-fine and 4/8 representations meet the specified max(1 cm, 5% y) oracle tolerance on every audited label, with no overflow. Coarser cells increase oracle MAE from 0.039102 to 0.154041 and maximum error from 21.39 to 59.55 m. The 4/8 codebook exchanges quantization resolution for smaller candidate set. second independently initialized model changes only these fine cardinalities. Choice, point, count, and angle implementations remain fixed; no length batching optimization is introduced in this quality comparison. The estimated scalar sequence length is bounded by 1,514 tokens. Training takes 1,369.33 seconds versus 1,604.98 for the prior 30-by-32 run under their recorded timing scopes. sections.content: H.1 Length Grouping Separates Padding from Rank Imbalance The final scheduling mechanism is defined in Section C.3. Its performance study holds global batch 256, microbatch 8, four accumulation steps, eight L20D GPUs, the old 72K data/codebook, and the timing instrumentation fixed. Four fresh runs each process 100 updates and 25,600 QA: original order, local length grouping, global grouping with rank balancing, and global balancing with 128-QA buffer. The last 92 updates contain the same 23,552 measured QA; the first eight are excluded for warmup. The buffer is drained at both measurement boundaries, and slow steps remain in the timing record. The controlled scheduling results are reported in Table 6. 35 Figure 7. Controlled scheduling comparison on the historical 72K corpus. Local grouping reduces padding but leaves more rank imbalance; global grouping and balancing deliver the largest throughput gain. cross-update buffer reduces padding slightly further without increasing throughput. Local grouping increases throughput from 99.06 to 116.91 QA/s and reduces padding from 35.17% to 12.36%. However, mean gradient-ready spread between ranks increases from 115.0 to 306.6 ms, and tail communication/wait time from 39.5 to 157.6 ms. Minimizing padding independently on each rank can therefore leave unequal workloads at synchronization. Global grouping plus balancing reduces padding to 1.77%, reduces ready-time spread relative to local grouping to 145.7 ms, and reaches 129.54 QA/s: 30.78% throughput increase or 23.53% less measured time for equal QA volume. Ready-time spread and tail time remain above the original-order values, so this gain reflects the combined scheduling changes rather than an isolated reduction in synchronization waiting. The 128-QA buffer lowers padding to 1.03% but achieves 129.39 QA/s. Its step-time coefficient of variation increases from 6.07% to 19.77%; even after aggregating pairs of updates into equal 512-QA units, variation is 6.30% versus 4.61% without the buffer. This identifies diminishing returns from further packing and supports the unbuffered final layout. Tail measurements include communication and waiting; no downstream accuracy evaluation is performed in these short runs. H.2 Microbatch Feasibility and Global Batch Size Table 26.
